SeriesStatAccessor::logcdf¶

Back to SeriesStatAccessor API Reference

Signatures¶

Series SeriesStatAccessor::logcdf() const
Series SeriesStatAccessor::logcdf(double sigma) const
Series SeriesStatAccessor::logcdf(double mu, double sigma) const
Series SeriesStatProxy::logcdf() const
Series SeriesStatProxy::logcdf(double sigma) const
Series SeriesStatProxy::logcdf(double mu, double sigma) const

What It Does¶

logcdf() returns log(P(X<=x)) for a normal model. It preserves information in extreme lower tails where cdf() may round probability to zero before a caller can take its logarithm.

Keeping Tail Evidence Finite¶

log(cdf(x)) is mathematically equivalent, but not numerically equivalent in the tail. logcdf() evaluates that quantity with tail-aware formulas, so a very unlikely event remains a large finite negative number rather than -inf.

Overloads choose standard normal, zero-mean custom sigma, or explicit mu,sigma. sigma must be positive.

Parameters And Returns¶

mu locates the model and sigma is its strictly positive standard deviation. The method standardizes each owner value using those parameters and returns a shape-preserving float64 Series. It performs no reduction and does not infer either parameter from the data.

Gradient¶

The derivative is the inverse Mills ratio pdf(x)/cdf(x). Reverse mode evaluates it through log-domain quantities so lower-tail sensitivities remain available when ordinary CDF values underflow.

Examples¶

Example 1. Ordinary points are natural logs of their CDF values.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-1.0, 0.0, 1.0});
std::cout << x.stat.logcdf() << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.8410216, -0.69314718, -0.17275378]

Example 2. Extreme tails stay represented.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({-20.0, -10.0, 10.0}).stat.logcdf() << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-203.91716, -53.231285, -7.619853e-24]

The value at -20 means the lower-tail probability is roughly exp(-203.9). Keeping the logarithm finite lets that evidence participate in later sums and comparisons even though ordinary probability space is near its limits.

Example 3. The reverse rule remains finite in that same lower tail.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-20.0, -10.0, 0.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.stat.logcdf().sum().reverse();
std::cout << x.sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[20.049753, 10.098093, 0.79788456]

The derivative grows in the far lower tail because a small movement in x causes a large relative change in an already tiny probability. The calculation uses exp(logpdf-logcdf) rather than dividing two underflowed ordinary values.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Output is a log probability and is therefore non-positive.

  • Use this method directly instead of calculating cdf().log() in tail work.

  • Large lower-tail gradients are mathematically meaningful, not an overflow by themselves; account for them when designing an objective.

  • sigma<=0 is invalid.

See Also¶

  • cdf: accumulated probability in ordinary scale.

  • logpdf: local density in log scale.
